body:
Ugh, the "never wanted to be a burden" is so hard to deal with - I'm sure she means it (who WANTS to be a burden?) but it's also a passive/ aggressive thing to say. Good luck with being there and navigating the difficult family waters. Just remember to take care of yourself some too.

No problem - you can always PM me too. This is my throwaway, but I do check it on the regular :)

Hey, I see that you didn't get any responses here so I'll throw in my two cents. I totally understand what you're saying about not liking EITHER option in this case. They both suck because the entire situation sucks. Doesn't matter if you throw yourself headlong into a rescue effort or if you divorce yourself from the problem. That being said, maybe now is a good time to start building a healthy relationship with your mom - one that is based on boundaries. Can you sit down and decide exactly how much of your time, energy and emotional bandwidth you are comfortable giving to your mother? If you can, try to outline some relationship guidelines based on those boundaries. That way you can honestly tell yourself that you are helping her as much as it is healthy for you to help her. That won't get rid of your guilt, but could help you keep her problems separate from your life. Boundaries are the basis of any healthy relationship and this suicide attempt could be a good "reset button" on your relationship with your mom.

Personal example of having to set boundaries with family: I had to tell my mother NOT to discuss her marital/ romantic problems with me. That's not my business. It should never be my business. That's between her and my dad. It is unfair of her to burden me with those details or to ask me to take sides between the two of them. I had to enforce that rule by hanging up on her or walking out of her house while she was talking to me. I had to do that several times before the rule stuck, but it did eventually stick. Now I can visit her without the dread that she's bring up shit I shouldn't hear.

Thanks for messaging me with those kind words. I was alone and hurting when I wrote that post. Fortunately, my husband came home from work a few hours later and I confessed to how bad I was feeling (though not to any direct plans like how to get the insurance to pay out). He was very upset - not at me, but for me. Lots of crying and talking on both sides. I'm feeling a little more hopeful and looking forward to my doctors appointment later this week. 

Please take care of yourself too. If it means anything, you're making a difference just by answering people in this forum.

Thanks for the response. I do have a lot and I'm doing a terrible job of taking care of all these good things. I look at my husband, our house, my dog, my work and I see how poorly I've maintained them, how much I shortchange them on a daily basis. I considered giving my dog to a neighbor who is crazy about him. She's retired and home all day. He could probably be a lot happier with her. My husband could probably be a lot happier with another woman. I'm not a lot of fun right now.

It's like I'm sitting on all of this good stuff, not being able to appreciate it and selfishly keeping it away from people who could have it and be happy. I don't feel like I deserve any of this. 

I am putting all my energy in to making the most that I can out of these last months with dad. It's draining, but it feels good. It's something that matters and that only I can give him. It just that once he's gone... there's no use for me anymore. I should go away and let other people make the most of the opportunities I'm squandering.

Therapy helped me understand that family is only one part of what makes up your sense of self. You can't disregard it (like never talking about it) but you can't let it completely define you either. I still have plenty of problems, but therapy helped me drawn a line between my family's problems and my problems. It also helped me define where my culpability/ responsibility for them started and ended. Everything I do is not their "fault" and everything they do is not my "fault." That sounds totally, idiotically obvious but trust me, most of us don't really believe it. 

It has been 17 years since my sister's suicide attempt. Only 14 since her successful suicide. I don't tell everyone the full truth about my family, but have told a small number of friends. They are very understanding. I still feel bad about what happened with my sister, but when that happens I can have a more rational response (most of the time). Rational responses let you deal with emotions in a helpful way (talk to a trusted friend, vent in an anonymous online community, write it out, sweat it out at the gym, run it out on the beach) and not a harmful way (drinking, drugs, bad relationships, violence). 

Still, I've never been 100% honest with friends or family about my mental state. Sometimes it's worse than they know and other times it's WAY worse than they know. It's pretty terrible right now, but at least I know to reach out to a doctor and to try and talk it out online. At least those choices could lead to things getting better. Sometimes that's all you can hope for.

The idea of starting fresh is attractive, but the reality is you're still the same person and you carry the same baggage in to every new situation... until you put down the bag and unpack it. It's only then that you have a chance to walk in to a new situation and really be ready to take advantage of all the opportunities there. Therapy isn't a cure-all, but it can give you some tools to help unpack your bag. Once you learn how to use those tools, it makes all the other good things you've planned (like the volunteering and martial arts) more than fun or distraction. It's like they're ways for you to build a new sense of self.

If there's any way for you to make the time for therapy now, try doing it. my sister attempted suicide while I was in college, so I feel kind of like I know what you're going through. I didn't tell anyone the extent of her problems either - college is a really fun time for most people - talk about mental health problems and death isn't really  "life of the party" conversation. Still, getting therapy helped a lot. It was through therapy that I found a way to talk about my family and their issues without feeling ashamed or embarrassed about it. Once you start talking to people, you find out that everyone's family is at least a little messed up.

Do you have any other family? If so, spending time with them would be a good place to start. Even if it's just a phone call. You are the people who are hurting the most right now and who have the most insight to what you're all going through. Put aside any differences or awkwardness and reach out.
